blocks.x: you see we're recording today in the seminar room to the Howard Tilton Library you see the day is April of what I can't remember
12 April
Tuesday is 11th that's right because I know the Eureka is playing tonight here on campus 1961 and let's get your name on here
you want me to give it?
mm-hmm
my name is William Ridgely and what's your name? my name is John Hampton
you just happened to be present and we got proof now you're guilty and I'm Dick Allen we're gonna play a record now for him Ridgely which he hadn't heard in how long haven't you?

This is Real 2, Bebe Ridgely, April 11th, 1961. Okay, we're gonna play a little more of Handy's saxophone now. Wrong there. Right at the head, maybe we can get rid of that horn. Wrong there. Wrong there.
This is Real 3 Baby Ridgely, April 11, 1961. See, we're talking about Tucker left for Chicago. Yeah, we were talking about Tucker and he left Chicago and that's me.
This is Real Thor, Bebe Ridgely, April 11th, 1961. I wondered about Louis Cottrell Jr., the clarinet player and saxophone player.
He played with me.
Where was that?

Let me see what time could that have been. He didn't stay too long. He was playing with me and another fellow came in. Let me see the name of my 20th player. He was playing with saxophone and Derby. He's dead. Arthur Derby is a violin player he was with me.
Derby is alive I believe. Is he?
Somebody told me he was dead. I saw him a couple of years ago.
He may be dead now. I don't know.
And so Louis hadn't been with me alone. This fellow came in and took Louis and Derby and broke up my band and went on off. I forgot that guy in there. He had a big band.
The trumpet player that went out to Texas?
Yeah. What's his name? Don Albert. Yeah. I want to show you a picture in a book over here. Has he still got his band?
No, no. He has a nightclub out there here.
Oh, I see. He was a good clarinet player.
Yeah, I believe he is. What they say about him. And he made a few records himself. Yeah.
He's a good band in the new one.

Let me find this picture if I can. There's a picture of your tuxedo band about 1925, it says. This is in Jazz, New Orleans, 1885-1957 by S.B. Charters. It's got Bill Matthews' picture on drums with you.
That's his brother.
That's not Bill, huh? No.
They call that Philip B.B.

Oh, yes. And it's got you and then it's got Schatz. Willie Joseph, that's Kaiser. Emma is sitting at the piano. Arthur Durbany. And a saxophone player from St. Louis. It looks like he's playing a tenor or a C melody. I can't tell for sure. Must be a tenor. And then Robert Hall is another saxophone player. Willie Bontong playing the banjo and somebody...
That must have been the one I was trying to tell you about there, you see, that saxophone player that I had when they went out. What's his name?
He doesn't give his name.
Well that might be him. I tried to have a voice in minor. That might be him.
He went to St. Louis. He's from St. Louis it says here, the saxophone player. And a guy called Jesse on tuba. I don't know who Jesse is. Big dog dog fella it looks like.
That's John Porter. Might be. That's where it is. We didn't have no other fella but John Porter.
It's an upright tuba. Yeah. John Porter. Let's see.
Got everything I've done up here man.
Yeah. Well we've been talking to you you know. What about Earl Fusche? Did you ever know him?

Yeah. Pretty good saxophone player. He played with me a while but he's another fella with a big head that couldn't get along with him. Thought he was going to saxophone player in town. I don't know what he'd come up in.
I think he's in California now. Yeah he left there already now.
But he went out and found I guess some saxophone players. He was pretty good here. When was he with you?

I don't know. Maybe we'll be able to tell you. Was he before Handy or? Before Handy or? I just can't get them together. Let's see. I think he was before Handy. Was it before he was with Sam Morgan or after? No, after he was with Morgan. Oh he made those records with Morgan in 27 I believe it was. So it would have to be after 27 then.
It was after Morgan because he came with our band because we were making more money in Morgan and he was glad to be with us but it was hard to get along with.
What about Albert French? Do you know him, the banjo player? Yeah I know him but he never played any of them. And what about Gilbert Young?

He played with him in a while. He got a big head until he still got it. He couldn't get along. I think when he couldn't divide, he tried to read and he couldn't play four quarters in the bar. At that way back there in slow time, all that. And he got so big I had to get rid of him.
How old was he?

He started with me when he was quite young, going to play second cornet. His boy had a good tone and he could make high notes and had a good drag time in his head and everything like that and I just thought maybe he made good enough. He was hard to get along with. Especially with my kind of a work I had.
Oh yeah. Was he working with you when Solistan was in your band?
He worked a little while but that's some playing second, not much.
Solistan was playing first?

Oh, Solistan was in my lifetime playing first. You see, Solistan leaving my band and I didn't care where he would go, I'd always have open for him. When he come back, well he got ready to come back to the band and they all well understood that. They never did try to keep them out. You know, if he got out of the job he used to come right on back. But we started together and both of us was coming to boys and I kept the band going. He used to come right on back whenever he got ready. He left me about three or four times. I fell down. That's how Amos got with me once and Mutt got with me once when he left. I said, Buddy Bacique got in there.
Could you give me that picture of Thomas' man?

Buddy, I didn't get rid of Buddy. Buddy got ready to set. Buddy told him I had too much weight for him. He said, you know what job he got on the riverfront? He said, my band had too much weight for him. I guess he wanted to set up his own band. That's all I feel.
Can you find me a picture of Louie Nelson, the trombone player? Over there in the files, he doesn't show in this one.
Trombone?
Yeah, trombone player.
Louie Nelson. Yeah.

What about Arnold Matoya? Did you ever use him? Well, he helped played with me. But he didn't like the idea of being with us much, you know. We didn't get too much about him. He was a real good corner player. Couldn't I use him? What did Buddy Petit play like? That always fascinates me. Oh, he was good.

That guy could play like anything. He was a real good corner player. He was a real good corner player. He was a real good corner player. Couldn't I use him? I don't like the idea of being with us much, you know. We didn't get too much about him. He was a real good corner player. Couldn't I use him? What did Buddy Petit play like? That always fascinates me.
Oh, he was good. That guy could play like anything.

He drank hard to get along with that time, you know. When he was sober, it was all right. But if he felt like drinking and didn't get what kind of job you have, he'd just go on to sleep and wouldn't send nobody. I remember once we had to go to Kenwood to play, and I don't know what's going to do. I don't know what's going to do. I don't know what's going to do. I remember once we had to go to Kenwood to play, and I live uptown, and we'd go down way down around Esplanade Street, and Jeremy and his women would get him to go out. We had a big job, you know. We'd go out for a week. A man would go to sleep on you and forget something like that to get you in trouble. But I had such a good grip among the people. Everywhere I went, Louisiana, Mississippi, most of my childhood never did have any trouble.
Must have been an awfully good going up for everyone. Buddy? Does anybody sound anything like Buddy?
Well, see, I don't pay much attention to things like that now, but Buddy was just named Buddy. He said more than Oliver Lewis.
You wouldn't remember what Buddy sounded like if you heard it? I'm going to see if I can find something more. Maybe he's...
I just wondered maybe this particular record sounds a little like Buddy. There's so many fellas tried to imitate his style too, you know.
Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm.
That's his style. What does it sound like?
That's a good one. Who?
That's funny. It ain't somebody just like you, but that's his style. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. That's just like him. Somebody show him and then imitate him.
Somebody imitate him is what I figured.
What's his style?
I hear that that's his style and I wanted you to tell me because I know you'd know.

That's his style. You know who played on his order? Who's that? The white boy got the band. What's his name now? Old, old, old musician. He'd be playing, making good money later. That's his name now. That's his name now. That's his name now. . You like Sash playing Star Ben South Stand?
But South Stand knew how to get along with the people, huh? I haven't think much of his playing.
No. He just had a good wonderful name. Mutt. Sash. Sash is good. Sweet. That's his star. If it ain't him, it's somebody much just like him.
He's so strong. Copy him.

That's every bit of his star. He was good. People used to ask for him all the time, but he just had that bad habit, you know. I understand he's such a nice fellow. People didn't like him. But Mutt and that boy, they'd ask for him all the time.
Oh, yeah. Yeah, that's interesting to hear that that really liked Buddy, huh?
Just liked him. He could just, he's now trombone player with Buddy, Buddy, he's learning how to make all of his part, and he could help everybody out in the band. He's just gifted.
When did they start playing by head in the street, in parades and funerals?

Well, the, you see, the Excelsior band and the Onward band, those bands from downtown, the old man George Moret was at Excelsior, and Manuel Perez was the Onward band. Well, those fellows always had, uh, reading musicians, see, they had better reading musicians downtown than they did uptown, see? They were real better musicians, plenty of them. And the most of the faking was from uptown, I guess. But that had been going on with them up there a long time. See, they go to Manmoretti and them and they ain't bad man. They knew if you did not read you couldn't play with them.
They had to play your voice.

And Manmoretti would be a whole lot like that, too. They always had all good reading men. But they were all good musicians from downtown, those Creole people. I knew them all because I worked in the country grocery in Jefferson, Paris. And it was about a mile and a quarter out of the city limit. And they used to hire those fellows. They played fumes and all like that and parades and everything. Well, I knew all those old musicians' names from Wike and that Stewart. I had to stop there to get where they was going, see. I'd know them. I used to take them in and give them a big cool drink of water and some of them. I'd give them a drink of whiskey. I had the privilege I could do that. And they all got to know me. I'd know them all of them once by then. People used to wonder how I know them all of them. That's from when I was in the country before I came to New Orleans. And I worked in the country grocery from about 11 years old until I got married and see, I'd wait for them for about 18 years. And then the people helped me along with my music business and helped me with everything. It was very good to me. I still even hit one of them.
But did they have any brass bands that just played by head uptown when you were a little boy?

No, no. They all were spelled. They had to read them. They had to read them. Somebody had to read to play them. Most of them. You couldn't handle no brass bands. They didn't. They weren't trying to play some marches and punes and things like that. They had to read, but some of them could fake. They were pretty good.
When did they start playing? They were playing fake numbers in the street like they do now.
I already knew them to do it.
They would always play some fake numbers.
They always did know them to do it.
Here's a picture. That's Paul Barnes.
Yes, it's here.
Can you see Lewis Nelson there, that trombone player?
I've seen him in the street, but I never did know him. You never did know him. No, but I still know him. Lately I've met him in the street. I recognize him there. Who is that?
That banjo player? No, right there. Trumpet player? That's Kid Thomas from across the river. Oh, I see. Paul Barnes. He never did come back. He didn't make it so good.

He never did come back. He didn't make it so good. Bonds is back here. I knew he did. Yeah, but he seems to have trouble with his clarinet playing. He can't play it like he… I know he's not doing what he thinks he can do. Yeah. He got himself rated a little above. He tried to come back and get me to set up a bunch of guards, but I didn't want to do it the same time.
No. I want to play a tape for you here, if I can find it.
Gee, it's starving out.
That's old baby Dodds there. Yeah.
All he was is dead now. Your brothers?
Your brothers played, you say? You told me before, your brothers played music, huh? My brothers?

Oh, yeah. But they started in the Spanish War, you know. They were musicians in the American-Spanish War, my two brothers, but they didn't play no dance music. No. Well, what bands did they play with?
They never played.
They didn't play with any band outside the Uncle Sam Band. Oh, yeah.
I thought maybe they played with some brass bands here or something.
No, no. No, no. No, no. I never did. Was Celestan as old as you or not? Well, you know, in the beginning I thought he was, but when he died he wasn't. I see.
He died. He grew younger instead of older.
Yeah, he grew younger, but Celestan was older than me.
That's funny. Where did you get educated, by the way? Where did you go to school? What school?
I went there. I went there. They cut the machine off that while then. Okay.
Well, you tell me you did go to school that while. But you might have done here. Mm-hm. If this sounds like an old-time band that you know of, the style that they're playing in…

That's like Bob Lyons and Frankie Deucing. That's like Bob Lyons and Frankie Deucing. Yeah, that's way back there. That's the old style way back on the center. They might not be an old musician, but it's sound.
Well, they're old. But that was only made about a year ago.
Yeah, June 12, 1960. Peter Bocas and Charlie Love.
There's a song that's trying to do at Montrum on the beat.
Tell Albert to want him.
Albert to want him.
He plays with the Eureka. You know him.
I know him. He's never the player anymore. He's too much to my time.
Peter Bocas and Charlie Love. Yeah, he's playing the violin. Yeah. Paul Bonds is playing the clarinet. Yeah. Manuel Sells on banjo. See what all you want. Good.

You boys, wonderful banjo jam. You see, Peter Bocas, if there's anything in there at all, in the train, he really can make you. Yeah. I don't mind you, but... See, I've only got something else to say about that, don't you?
Guitar, no. Did you know Sails? When you were playing music, did you know him very well?
Now he was, Sails was on the boat with us. He was on the boat with us?
Yeah. You mean when Baby Dodge was with you?
Well, yeah. May I say that, did he? I believe he was on that boat with us.
With Faye, huh?
I think he was, yeah. He's a smart kid.
Well, he ought to be talented. His father must have been a pretty good guitar player.
He was.
Did he ever work with you in your band, Sails?
Yes, right.
Regular?

Yeah. He worked with us. Sails worked with us until we got on the boat. That's where he got a job on the boat, and he never would come back anymore, you know? I mean, I don't even call it. I worked with many of them.
Sails was old enough to play with you in 1918 or so during the war?
Yeah, yeah. Sure.
He sure doesn't look old. Mm-hmm.
Your daddy looked good, and he was an old man.
Mm-hmm. I see. Did you ever know George Field?
Yeah. George Field, I wait. I knew him.
He was a trombone player. He went up to Chicago.
That's the man that I was trying to get to hear about. George Field. That's the man. That's the first trombone player, George Field. I'll say to you something else.
You said Tucker.
Tucker was a trombone player too, but I know George Field.
And when did he start playing Sly?

Well, I was a little bit of a boy when I knew him playing slide trombone. That's right. George Field. George Field played for Sly Stanton in the district at the Tuxedo Hall. He was a good trombone player, a real good one. He helped Sly Stanton a whole lot. But the man Tucker right there went long before him. Yeah. Tucker. Yeah, George Field, that's right. So he was a good trombone player, a good musician.
Remember Eddie Atkins? Yeah, he was a good trombone player. Who did they work with?
Eddie Atkins worked with Joe Oliver for a long time. Down here? Yeah. They had a good band. He's there too, huh?
Yes, he is. I've been to his grave. They buried out in Amor, up near Wagamon.

Somewhere. Eddie was a good trombone player. He's buried in the same graveyard as Joe Avery. At that time him and Nora and this other boy, he died, or he must have died with. Now he was a good trombone, Zoo. Zoo? Yeah. Zoo Robertson? Yeah. He was a good trombone player. Who did he work with? He was a Batalier's nephew. Batalier taught him trombone in the beginning. He worked in bands, right, but he played in those cyclic bands until he was a weird familiar up at the time like that. He didn't stay on my own. He was good. He was good. That's right. What about Roy Palmer? Who did he play with? He used to play, him and I, in Tuxedo band together, Palmer trombone. He left here a long time too. In the brass band? Yeah, in the brass band. Did he play dance work too? Oh yeah. He played dance work, but he never was lucky enough to get in a good band now, because that's why he left. But he's a pretty good player.
He's a good player. He had a good sense of humor too. He could play funny stuff. Fast execution here. We've got records with him on it too, if you want to hear them.
He's still at home. I haven't wait to play for so long. Well let me dig one out for you now.
All right, you've got everybody. No, I wish we did have everybody. A lot of them never made records.
You've got them. I forgot all about them. Just like they think about me, I think some of them did. They think the same thing about me. They haven't wait for me for so long.
Well, Roy, I think it's, last time I heard, is still working in a steel mill and strong, you know?

They tell me he's got a nice job. I don't think he ever came back here in New Orleans. But I've never lived in New Orleans over, I was gone 30 days. I've never lived this over 30 days. Where did you go when you left? On the boat. On the boat, huh? Yeah. Yes, Roy. I came back. I've been here all of my life.
Where did you go? Where did you go? Where did you go? That's it. That's it.
That's it. That's it.
That's it. That's it. That's it. That's it.
That's it.
That's it. I'll be good. I'm sorry he quit playing. I'll be good. I'll be good.
I'll be good.
Let's see. What about his executions compared with Kid Ari in those times? Did Ari execute as fast as Roy?
No. Good role. Good role. No. Good role. No, it was good. But from what Roy is doing there now, Roy didn't get up to that. Roy got a little of everything on that from there now.
Well that's twenty years ago when that was, I mean- Twenty years ago. No, more than that, no. Yeah.
Closer to, over thirty years ago he was doing that. Roy was good. But their style at that time wasn't, he didn't come up to what Roy is doing there now. What about Jack Carey?
Did he come up to that?
He was good. He was good. He was on that auditory. Jack was on that auditory. Mm-hmm. Pretty rough, huh?
Yeah, rough.
Rough. Real rough. All of them were rough. Thank you to them were rough.
I wanted to ask you why you stopped playing at the Boston Club. Exactly what happened?
I didn't stop playing at the Boston Club. You see, they didn't take my job from me after Celestine died.
Mm-hmm.
But I quit, I think, to join church.
Oh, I see. I see.

I just quit and give it up. I've become a member of the church and I've been there ever since. I've been everything but the preacher in the church and I didn't try to do that because I wasn't enough of that.
Mm-hmm.

I was a class leader. I helped in the choir when they need somebody. I'm on the Stuart bench, you know, in the church. So I'm praying the rest of my years, my 30 years, right in the church, just like I did when I was playing music.
Oh, when you quit, who did you give your music to? What did you give him?

Followed by the name of, we didn't know him nothing else but by Red. He didn't live here. He used to go, every year he'd come through on a cycle, see, like that. And we got to know him whenever he'd come, he'd always talk with us. So last time, before I stopped playing, he came through and I wanted to quit because I began to get pyreia, you know. And I asked him about taking my place in the band. And he said that he had to go to Tulsa, Oklahoma. That's where this band, the Psych is at. And he would write me when he got there and he did that. And so I wrote for him to come. He came in his home, it was kind of bad. And I let him use my own and he offered the bite and I sold it to him, see, for $25. I paid $192, I think that's $192 and a half, something like that for him. And I never did give him $5,000, I never did see him anymore. I haven't seen him since.
I'm afraid it's about to run out now.
Well, I think it's all right.
Yeah, so we'll just let it run on out. We still appreciate it.
He was back here in New Orleans. We never did, I never did see him anymore. So when I stopped playing music, I got rid of everything. I said, the gas and water didn't mix.

segments.title: Recording setup and date, April 1961
segments.summary: Allen and Ridgley settle the date, announce the recording at the Tilton Library seminar room and give names for the tape.

segments.title: Reel 2 and 3 announcements, Handy's saxophone record
segments.summary: Reel announcements, playing a record of Handy's saxophone, and a mention of Tucker leaving for Chicago.

segments.title: Louis Cottrell Jr., Arthur Derbigny and Don Albert breaking up the band
segments.summary: Ridgley says Cottrell played with him briefly, and that Don Albert took Cottrell and Derbigny and broke up his band.

segments.title: Identifying the men in a Charters photo of the Tuxedo band
segments.summary: Allen reads out the names in a c.1925 Tuxedo band photo; Ridgley corrects the drummer and recalls the tuba player John Porter.

segments.title: Earl Fouche and Gilbert Young as hard-to-handle sidemen
segments.summary: Ridgley describes Fouche and Gilbert Young as good players with big heads who were hard to work with; Young started young on second cornet.

segments.title: Celestin leaving and returning; Buddy Petit leaving the band
segments.summary: Ridgley says Celestin played first cornet, left about three or four times and was always welcome back; others like Buddy left to start their own band.

segments.chapter: Buddy Petit and brass band reading
segments.title: Buddy Petit's playing and his unreliability
segments.summary: Ridgley and Allen discuss Buddy Petit as a versatile cornetist who drank, would oversleep and miss jobs.

segments.chapter: Buddy Petit and brass band reading
segments.title: Listening to a record for Buddy Petit's style
segments.summary: While a record plays they debate whether it is Buddy Petit or an imitator; Ridgley says people loved Buddy despite his bad habits.

segments.chapter: Buddy Petit and brass band reading
segments.title: Downtown reading bands versus uptown faking in brass bands
segments.summary: Ridgley says the Excelsior and Onward bands downtown had reading musicians while most faking came from uptown, and recalls the musicians he met working at a country grocery as a boy.

segments.chapter: Buddy Petit and brass band reading
segments.title: Photos of Paul Barnes, Kid Thomas and Louis Nelson
segments.summary: Looking at photos, they identify Paul Barnes and Kid Thomas; Ridgley says Barnes never made it back and had clarinet trouble.

segments.title: Baby Dodds tape, Ridgley's brothers and Celestin's age
segments.summary: A Baby Dodds tape is mentioned, Ridgley's brothers were Spanish-American War musicians, and Celestin turns out to be older than Ridgley.

segments.title: Schooling and listening to a 1960 old-style band recording
segments.summary: A question about school goes unanswered; Ridgley hears a June 1960 recording with Peter Bocage and Charlie Love and calls it the old style.

segments.title: Guitarist Sails on the riverboat and in Ridgley's band
segments.summary: Ridgley says Sails worked in his band, then took a riverboat job and did not return; they discuss his age and his father.

segments.title: Trombonists George Fields and Tucker
segments.summary: Ridgley recalls George Fields as the first trombone player he knew, playing in the district, and says Tucker was earlier.

segments.title: Eddie Atkins, Zue Robertson and Roy Palmer
segments.summary: Ridgley recalls Atkins with Joe Oliver, Zue Robertson taught by Batiste, and Roy Palmer in the Tuxedo brass band.

segments.title: Roy Palmer's fast execution and Jack Carey
segments.summary: They discuss Roy Palmer working in a steel mill, how he compares for speed to earlier players, and Jack Carey; Ridgley says he always stayed in New Orleans apart from boat trips.

segments.title: Leaving the Boston Club and joining the church
segments.summary: Ridgley says he quit playing after Celestin died to join the church, where he became class leader and sang in the choir.

segments.title: Selling his instrument to Red and giving up music
segments.summary: Ridgley sold his horn to a traveling player called Red for $25 and never saw him again; the tape runs out.
